newsitem.title: BRAZIL: French eye Brazil telecoms, await new sector rules.
newsitem.headline: French eye Brazil telecoms, await new sector rules.

text.p: French companies interested in a slice of Brazil's fast-growing telecommunications market are waiting for the Brazilian government to draft new rules governing the sector before deciding on their investment strategies, officials said.

Representatives of 25 companies, in Sao Paulo for a telecommunications seminar sponsored by the French Consulate, said they were seeking partners and investment opportunities in Brazil's lucrative and soon-to-be privatized telecom sector.
However, they said a new law governing the sector -- a draft of which is is due out in late October -- is key to defining their plans.

"Brazil is one of the biggest markets in the world for telecommunications, so there's a lot of interest in the new rules," said Didier Guigon, Latin America sales manager for Bell Laboratories' TRT-Lucent Technologies.
Leading companies such as Alcatel Alsthom, which will invest $250 million this year, want to see the new regulations before setting out its Brazilian investment plans for next year.
"Everyone is waiting for the rules of the game," said Guilherme Athia, marketing and communications director for Alcatel's Brazilian unit, Alcatel Telecomunicacoes SA.
Later this year, Brazil plans to begin transferring its huge telecommunications sector to private hands, starting with the sell-off of the B Band cellular frequency.

The privatization of federally owned telecoms giant Telebras and its 28 subsidiaries is expected to begin in 1997. Among those interested in the sales are the world's largest telecommunications firms, including companies from Asia, Europe and United States.
Brazil expects to draw $7 billion in telecommunications investments by 2003, according to government figures.
"Growth will be explosive, that's why we want to be in here now," said Didier Lesbre, export director for Latin America and Africa for France's Matra Marconi Space.
Guigon of Lucent, which sells wireless local loop technology, said the new rules promise to strip away limits on foreign participation in the sector.
Other companies with representatives at the seminar included France Telecom, Bull SA, Aerospatiale, Citcom, Dassault A.T. and Thomson-CSF Communications/RSC.
France accounts for 2 percent to 3 percent of Brazilian exports and is the fifth-largest investor in Brazil.
